name: Esther Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Can you start by telling me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Esther, I'm 27, and I'm a senior motor claims handler at Brookvale Mutual, a small insurer owned by its members. I've got a history degree that I never used, and I fell into claims six years ago and turned out to be good at it. I rent a one-bed flat above a bakery on Mill Street, on my own. Money is tight, honestly, because the pay here is lower than in the city and I send a bit to my mum every month.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in by eight, and the first hour is the overnight car claims: photos, police numbers, garage estimates, the lot. I check each one against the policy wording on paper, with my own checklist that I've used since my first year, and I sign off the tricky ones the juniors can't. What I like is the phone calls, when someone has just written off their car and they need a real person to tell them what happens next. What wears me out is the system, which crashes twice a week and loses half my notes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say at union meetings: told you so, it was a sales pitch. I'd probably put something sharp in our branch group chat about all the money the bosses spent on consultants. Gwen (my lunch friend at work) would laugh and tell me to calm down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job would be fine, but my life would still be tight. I'd still be on lower pay than the city firms, with less than a month's rent in the bank, and that doesn't change because the robots stayed in the box. The routine bits, like logging the photos, might go to a program, and I'd have to put up with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd keep doing my job the way I do it now. I'd push the union to use the time to argue for a proper pay rise, because Brookvale can't claim the machines are coming for us anymore. I'd try to put aside fifty a month, which I've said every year and never managed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly, but not happy. The worry I carry every month is rent and my mum, not computers. AI going quiet doesn't make the boiler in my flat any less broken.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the routine logging might go to a program. How would you feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hate it, if I'm honest, because I don't trust it. When a junior logs photos wrong, I can see why and fix it, but a program just does it wrong quietly. I'd keep my paper checklist anyway, even if they told me not to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would worry you first in a bad month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rent, always the rent, because my landlord Mr Okafor puts it up every January. After that it's the car insurance, which is funny given where I work. I've skipped my mum's money once, and I felt sick about it for weeks.

say: I'd tell the union branch the **AI hype** was a sales pitch all along.
I'd say the bosses should spend the consultant money on **pay rises** for claims staff instead.
think: My **job is safe** here, but lower pay and almost no savings still keep me tight.
Losing the **routine logging** to a program would annoy me, because I don't trust it to get things right.
do: **Keep working** the way I do now, with my own paper checklist.
**Push the union** to ask Brookvale for a pay rise this year.
Try to **save £50 a month**, which I've never managed before.
feel: **Relieved** that the machines stayed small, but still **worn down** by rent and money.
S0.quote: AI going quiet doesn't make the boiler in my flat any less broken.
fieldNote: Her worries are **money first**: rent, a thin cushion and the money she sends her mum.
She is openly **distrustful** of software and would keep her paper checklist even if told to stop.
Union talk comes easily to her; it is her **main lever** for change.

steps.text: Keep checking motor claims with her own paper checklist
Ask the union branch to press Brookvale for a pay rise
Put aside £50 a month toward a rent cushion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be loud about it, I know myself. I'd say that claims handling is about people on the worst day of their year, and you don't hand that to a chatbot. I'd want the union to demand that nobody loses their job without retraining paid for by Brookvale.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think my job is exactly the sort that goes. Checking a garage estimate against a policy is checking, and that's on the list you read out. I'm senior, but that might just make me the expensive one, and there's no other insurer within an hour's drive of here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union meeting and get our branch to fight for a deal on job cuts. I'd cut my spending hard, no takeaways, cancel the gym, and try to get two months' rent saved. I know I should learn the new system, but I'd probably drag my feet until they made me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, really. I lie awake about rent already, and this would make it every night. It's not like I can pack up and move to the city on what I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd drag your feet on the new system. Why, if your job might depend on it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learning the new system feels like helping Brookvale replace me. I know that's stubborn, and my mum says so too. But I've watched them bring in two new systems already, and both times the team got smaller afterwards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gwen, mainly, because she's fifty-four and has done the same desk for twenty years. If they cut the team, they'll offer her early retirement on a pittance. I'd worry about the juniors as well, because their jobs are the first ones the software will swallow.

say: I'd say claims are about people on their **worst day**, not work for a chatbot.
I'd ask the union to demand **paid retraining** before anybody loses their job.
think: Checking **garage estimates** is exactly the sort of task this software takes first.
Being senior may just make me the **expensive one**, with no other insurer within an hour.
do: **Attend every union meeting** and push for a deal on job cuts.
**Cancel the gym** and takeaways to save two months' rent.
**Delay learning** the new claims system until management makes it compulsory.
feel: **Scared**, because the rent worry she already has would turn into a **nightly** one.
S1.quote: Learning the new system feels like helping Brookvale replace me.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose her job** and has no local insurer to move to.
Her resistance is **principled and emotional**: two past systems shrank the team, so she reads every new tool as a threat.
She worries about older colleagues and juniors as much as herself, which fits her **union** outlook.

steps.text: Attend every union meeting and push for a job-cuts agreement
Cancel the gym and takeaways to save two months' rent
Hold off on the new claims system until training is compulsory

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd stop saying anything polished and just say it's wrong. I'd be posting about it, sharing petitions, telling everyone that the government let this happen with no plan. At work I'd say what everyone else would be saying, which is: what happens to us?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm finished in claims by 2028 and I have nothing to fall back on. My whole job is reading, checking and deciding, so I don't even get the extra three years the plumbers get. That's all thinking work. I've got less than a month saved and no other skills that anybody pays for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know, and that's the frightening part. I'd join any campaign for a basic income or job guarantee, and I'd ask my mum if I could move back in with her if the flat goes. I suppose I'd look at care work, because that's hands-on and people still need it, but I've never done it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor going out from under me. I'm someone who likes things the same, and this is everything changing at once. I think I'd just freeze.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mum if you had to move back home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I'm sorry, because I'm meant to be the one helping her now. Her flat only has one bedroom, so I'd be on the sofa at twenty-eight. I'd probably cry, and she'd make tea and tell me it's not my fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned care work. Have you thought that through, or is it more of a hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a hope, really, I haven't looked into it at all. I know care homes are always hiring and they pay badly, worse than claims. But in that world it's one of the few things I can picture a person still doing in 2029.

say: I'd say the government let **AGI arrive** with no plan for people like us.
I'd share **petitions** and ask at work what happens to the claims team.
think: My job is all **thinking work**, so I don't even get the three extra years.
With **under a month saved** and no other paid skills, I have nothing to fall back on.
do: **Sign up** to any campaign for a basic income or job guarantee.
Ask her mum about **moving back home** if she loses the flat.
Look at **care work**, without having researched it yet.
feel: Like the **floor going out** from under her, with an urge to **freeze**.
S2.quote: My whole job is reading, checking and deciding, so I don't even get the extra three years the plumbers get.
fieldNote: She has **no plan** and no money to make one, which is why this reads as panic.
She understands the **thinking-first timing** clearly and sees it hits her straight away.
Moving home would reverse her role as the one **helping her mum**, which hurts most.

steps.text: Join a campaign for a basic income or job guarantee
Ask her mum about sleeping on the sofa if the flat goes
Look up care home jobs near Mill Street

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years and we should use them, which means the union, the government and Brookvale all sitting down now. I'd be the annoying one at every meeting asking what the plan is. Online I'd share stories of people who already lost jobs to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough time to see AGI coming and not quite enough to do anything about it on my money. I'd be 32 when it arrives, with nothing saved unless something changes. I'd know my claims job was ending and I'd still be sitting in it, because leaving early feels like giving up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first two years to save, even if it's only a hundred a month, by moving somewhere cheaper. I'd look into a care certificate at the college on Mill Street in the evenings, which I think is a year part-time. I'd be at union meetings pushing for redundancy terms that give people a year's pay, not three months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dread, but a slower dread. Like knowing an exam is coming that you haven't revised for. Some days I'd probably just pretend it wasn't happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said leaving early feels like giving up. Can you say more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm good at this job, properly good, and I worked to get senior at 25. Walking away from that before they push me feels like admitting the people who say it's all over were right. I know that's pride, but it's what I'd feel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would moving somewhere cheaper actually look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a shared house on Linden Road where a girl from the bakery rents a room. I'd lose my own front door, which I love, but I'd save about two hundred a month. I'd hate it for a year and then I'd get used to it.

say: I'd say we have **five years**, so the union, government and Brookvale should plan now.
I'd share **real stories** of people who already lost jobs to AI.
think: Five years lets me **see it coming** but not afford to do much about it.
I'd probably **stay in claims** until pushed, because leaving early feels like giving up.
do: **Move** to a **shared house** on Linden Road to save £200 a month.
**Study a care certificate** part-time at the local college in the evenings.
**Push the union** for redundancy terms worth a year's pay.
feel: A **slow dread**, like an exam she hasn't **revised** for.
S3.quote: Five years is enough time to see AGI coming and not quite enough to do anything about it on my money.
fieldNote: The extra time turns her panic into **planning**, but money still limits every option.
**Pride** in reaching senior at 25 makes her reluctant to leave before she is pushed.
She would trade her **own front door** for savings, which shows she is serious.

steps.text: Move into a shared house on Linden Road to save £200 a month
Take a part-time care certificate at the local college
Push the union for redundancy pay of a full year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance to do this properly, if the people in charge actually use it. I'd want a law that firms using AI have to pay for retraining. At work I'd say it the same way I say everything, which is bluntly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years means I can still have a working life I recognise for a while. I'd be 37 when it arrives, which is young enough to start again. But I know me, and I'd waste the first five years telling myself it wasn't real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Brookvale, because I'd need the wage, and I'd try to become the person who checks the AI's claim decisions for complaints. I'd save properly, maybe a hundred a month, and go for the care certificate later rather than sooner. I'd get the union to start talking to the company now, not in year nine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but it feels like there's room to breathe. I still wouldn't sleep great. But I'd feel like I had some say in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd check the AI's decisions for complaints. Isn't that using the AI you don't trust?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, and I know that sounds like a contradiction. Checking the AI's mistakes is the bit I'd actually be good at, because I don't trust it. Someone suspicious should be doing that job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop telling yourself it wasn't real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably seeing Gwen's desk go, or the juniors not being replaced when they leave. I need to see it happen to someone I know. Headlines don't move me, people do.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a real chance if people in charge use it.
I'd want a **law** making firms that use AI pay for workers' retraining.
think: At **37** I'd be young enough to start again when AGI arrives.
I'd probably **waste five years** telling myself it wasn't real.
do: **Stay at Brookvale** for the wage and aim for a role checking AI decisions.
**Save £100 a month** and take the care certificate later.
Get the union **talking to management** early, not in year nine.
feel: **Worried**, but with **room to breathe** and some say in what happens.
S4.quote: Checking the AI's mistakes is the bit I'd actually be good at, because I don't trust it.
fieldNote: She turns her **distrust** of AI into a possible job, a neat twist she noticed herself.
She admits she would **delay** acting until something happens to a colleague she knows.
The decade gives her **some control**, but her job still goes, so she stays anxious.

steps.text: Apply for a role checking AI claim decisions at Brookvale
Save £100 a month from her claims wage
Get the union branch to open talks with management now

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt, because it's my whole job in two years with no money behind me. What would help is a guarantee that people get paid while they retrain, like a year's wage. Not a voucher for an online course, an actual wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who gets the savings. If Brookvale cuts half the claims team, the members should get cheaper policies or the staff should get a share. Otherwise it's just the same people getting richer while I'm on my mum's sofa.

headlineQuote: If Brookvale cuts half the claims team, the members should get cheaper policies or the staff should get a share.
portrait: Esther is a 27-year-old senior **motor claims** handler at a small mutual insurer, renting alone on **thin savings**.
She is a committed **union** member who distrusts new software and works from her own paper checklist.
She stays uneasy even in AI Plateau, because **rent and her mum** already stretch her money.
AGI by 2028 leaves her **panicked**, while ten years' warning gives her room to plan care training.
She keeps asking **who gets the savings** when insurers replace claims staff with AI.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because her whole job goes in two years with **no money** behind her.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid year** of retraining, an actual wage rather than a voucher for an online course.
